claim: Large minibatches on ImageNet cause optimization difficulty rather than poor generalization: once the difficulty is addressed, there is no loss of accuracy up to minibatch 8,192.
stance_target: The repo's claim that large global batches are usable and that the constraint is optimization, not generalization
scope_conditions: ImageNet, ResNet-50, SGD with momentum, minibatch sizes up to 8,192 images
quoted_support: In this paper, we empirically show that on the ImageNet dataset large minibatches cause optimization difficulties, but when these are addressed the trained networks exhibit good generalization. Specifically, we show no loss of accuracy when training with large minibatch sizes up to 8192 images.

claim: The recipe has two parts: a hyperparameter-free linear learning-rate scaling rule (LR proportional to minibatch size) and a gradual warmup over the first epochs that overcomes early optimization problems.
stance_target: The mechanism the repo relies on when it raises the global batch to 1M tokens
scope_conditions: SGD with momentum, ImageNet; linear scaling plus warmup
quoted_support: To achieve this result, we adopt a hyper-parameter-free linear scaling rule for adjusting learning rates as a function of minibatch size and develop a new warmup scheme that overcomes optimization challenges early in training.

claim: With the recipe, ResNet-50 trains at minibatch 8,192 on 256 GPUs in one hour while matching small-minibatch accuracy, at about 90% scaling efficiency from 8 to 256 GPUs.
stance_target: Whether large-batch training actually converts into wall-clock throughput rather than only into fewer steps
quoted_support: With these simple techniques, our Caffe2-based system trains ResNet-50 with a minibatch size of 8192 on 256 GPUs in one hour, while matching small minibatch accuracy. Using commodity hardware, our implementation achieves ∼90% scaling efficiency when moving from 8 to 256 GPUs.

claim: Warmup is mandatory, not optional: the linear scaling rule alone does not work, and the paper presents warmup as the mechanism that overcomes early optimization difficulties.
stance_target: The repo's batch plan, which currently has no warmup phase for its 1M-token global batch
scope_conditions: ImageNet, SGD with momentum; lower learning rates at the start of training
quoted_support: To successfully apply this rule, we present a new warmup strategy, i.e., a strategy of using lower learning rates at the start of training [16], to overcome early optimization difficulties.

claim: The paper attributes large-batch problems to optimization difficulty rather than to generalization loss, explicitly contradicting the small-batch-is-better-generalization position.
stance_target: Masters and Luschi's claim that large batches inherently degrade generalization
scope_conditions: ImageNet classification; ResNet-50; SGD with momentum
quoted_support: Our comprehensive experiments in §5 show that optimization difficulty is the main issue with large minibatches, rather than poor generalization (at least on ImageNet), in contrast to some recent studies [20].

claim: The linear scaling rule and warmup generalise beyond classification to object detection and instance segmentation via Mask R-CNN.
stance_target: Whether the recipe is a general property of SGD training rather than an ImageNet artefact
scope_conditions: Mask R-CNN on COCO-style detection and segmentation tasks
quoted_support: Additionally, we show that the linear scaling rule and warmup generalize to more complex tasks including object detection and instance segmentation [9, 31, 14, 28], which we demonstrate via the recently developed Mask R-CNN [14].

claim: The evidence base is SGD with momentum on vision tasks, so the linear rule does not transfer directly to Adam-based LLM pretraining - Merrill et al. (2025) argue Adam needs square-root scaling instead.
stance_target: Whether the repo can cite Goyal et al. as support for its Adam-based 1M-token batch plan
scope_conditions: Scope limitation: ImageNet/COCO, SGD with momentum, ResNet-50 and Mask R-CNN
quoted_support: While this guideline is found in earlier work [21, 4], its empirical limits are not well understood and informally we have found that it is not widely known to the research community.
